newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh ruling party, opposition lock horns.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh ruling party, opposition lock horns.

text.p: Bangladesh on Sunday marked the first anniversary of the downfall of the previous government, with the opposition accusing the current administration of corruption.

The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) of former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia said it would announce plans on Monday to force the the "corrupt, inefficient and terrorist" government from power.
The Awami League of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said the BNP was taking a "destructive line" because it was unable to face opponents politically.
Independent analysts said it was now clear that the country's two largest parties were heading for a show of strength.
"Should that happen, the first victims would be the innocent people and the country's nsacent economy," one analyst said.

The BNP referred to Saturday's killing of a party worker in southeastern Feni town during a fight with Awami activists as "one of hundreds of such incidents that exposed the government's terrorist character@.

"The time has come for us to react aptly and stop them (Awami league) before it is too late," one BNP leader told Reuters. "We are promising the government a tough time ahead," said the leader who declined to be identified.
The BNP organised a countrywide strike on March 23, the first since Hasina took office last June, in which two people were killed and over 200 injured.
Khaleda, the country's first woman prime minister, resigned on March 30, 1996, during a stormy opposition campaign, that paved way for the June election under a neutral caretaker government.
Led by the then opposition Awami League, the campaign featured a series of violent general strikes and other protests which were backed by the country's powerful bureaucracy.
Hasina and Khaleda, both of whom sailed into politics by using the mantle of their late relatives, have since hardly smiled at each other.
Hasina's father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the country's independence leader, was killed in a 1975 army coup with most of his family.
Khaleda's husband former president general Ziaur Rahman was gunned down in another mutiny in 1981.

"On this day a year ago the people...installed democratic government under leadership of Sheikh Hasina. Let us renew our pledge today not to allow any undemocratic and anti-people force to take over again," Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad told a meeting of Awami League in Dhaka on Sunday.
Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak said: "A conspiracy is being hatched to negate the successes of Sheikh Hasina's government. This has to be resisted and democracy preserved."
The BNP has opposed all plans of Hasina, including the recent signing of the Ganges water sharing treaty with India.
It has decried the government's plans to give India a land transit through Bangladesh to reach its northeastern states and buy electricity from India to overcome domestic shortfall.
Khaleda called for mass resistence against Hasina. The BNP has already mustered support in its campaign from several small but militant parties, including those headed by Islamic fundamentalists.
